headline: The Missile Defense Agency has awarded Lockheed Martin a $211.4 million contract modification to build new Configuration 3 (C3) THAAD launchers for the United Arab Emirates (UAE) under a Foreign Military Sales (FMS) agreement. The move is intended to strengthen the UAE’s ballistic missile defense capability while allowing its THAAD launchers to be more widely dispersed across the country. The significance of Configuration 3 goes beyond simply adding more launchers. It is part of THAAD’s broader hardware and software modernization, bringing improvements to cybersecurity and Link 16 communications while enhancing the system’s ability to integrate with a wider range of sensors. This is particularly important for the UAE, where key targets, including air bases, ports, population centers, energy facilities, and logistics infrastructure, are spread across a relatively large area. Recent regional missile attacks have demonstrated that effective interception is only part of the equation. Maintaining sufficient interceptor reserves and the ability to sustain defensive operations through multiple attack waves are equally critical. With the growing threat from ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones across the Middle East, the UAE is moving toward a more dispersed, interconnected, and resilient air defense architecture.

headline: An Italian Eurofighter assigned to NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission shot down a drone of unconfirmed, but likely Russian origin after it entered Latvian airspace Friday, according to NATO and Latvian authorities. Two Italian Eurofighters scrambled from Lithuania along with two Turkish F-16s from Estonia. One of the Italian jets identified and engaged the drone. Latvian forces are now searching for the wreckage near Rugāji, about 35 km from the Russian border, so the drone’s origin has not yet been established. The incident comes amid a growing number of drone incursions into Baltic airspace. Latvia says Ukrainian drones have entered the region several times this year, while officials also point to Russian electronic warfare as a possible factor causing Ukrainian systems to stray across borders. Before Friday's incident, Ukrainian forces had launched attacks against Russian ports near St. Petersburg. Russian authorities claimed to have intercepted 15 Ukrainian drones during those attacks. This is the third reported NATO interception of a drone in the Baltics in recent months, following a Romanian F-16 shootdown in Estonia in May and a French Rafale shootdown in Latvia in June.

headline: President Donald J. Trump has issued a memorandum directing a major overhaul of U.S. Navy shipbuilding, citing cost growth, delays, design complexity and insufficient industrial capacity. Among the key directives: • CVN-81: Within 60 days, the administration will develop a plan to replace the EMALS electromagnetic catapult system and Advanced Weapons Elevators with traditional steam and hydraulic systems. • Foreign shipbuilding: The administration will pursue a "Finland Model" allowing foreign shipbuilders to participate in up to three ship classes, provided they build or acquire a U.S. shipyard, train an American workforce, transfer relevant technology and establish a U.S. supply chain. The first two ships could be built overseas, with subsequent ships built in the United States. • New surface combatants: The Navy will develop a new competitive acquisition approach for affordable, mature-design surface combatants capable of anti-submarine warfare, surface warfare and convoy escort. • Fifth Navy shipyard: A plan will be developed for a fifth public Navy yard, including additional drydock capacity for nuclear-powered submarines and aircraft carriers. • Submarine repair: The administration will establish a Component Repair Center intended to maintain at least one complete set of spare equipment for the Los Angeles, Virginia, Seawolf, Ohio and Columbia classes. • NAVSEA reform: The Naval Sea Systems Command will undergo a review aimed at reducing bureaucracy, increasing accountability and preventing repeated redesigns of mature ship designs. The memorandum's overarching objective is to increase U.S. shipbuilding capacity and competition while reducing the cost and time required to build and maintain Navy vessels. Importantly, most of these provisions direct the Department of War and Navy to develop plans within specified timelines; they do not themselves immediately authorize or fund construction of the projects described.

headline: President Trump has directed the Navy to abandon the electromagnetic aircraft launch system (EMALS) being used on the Gerald R. Ford class carriers and return to traditional steam catapults, according to U.S. officials cited by the Wall Street Journal. Trump signed a national security memorandum directing the Navy to redesign the fourth Ford class carrier, Doris Miller, and subsequent ships around steam catapults. The first three carriers, Gerald R. Ford, John F. Kennedy and Enterprise, will retain EMALS. The decision reverses years of Navy and industry resistance to Trump's proposal, largely because replacing EMALS would require significant redesign and could cost billions of dollars. Trump has criticized EMALS for years, arguing that it is overly complex and less reliable than steam catapults. The move effectively locks in a major technological reversal for future U.S. aircraft carriers. Source: https://www.wsj.com/us-news/trump-orders-navy-to-restore-old-technology-in-aircraft-carriers-costing-billions-0055ec1b?mod=hp_lead_pos2

headline: Lawmakers are demanding answers from the U.S. Navy amid reports of a mental health crisis, including multiple attempted suicides, onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) currently deployed to the Middle East to support military operations and the ongoing naval blockade against Iran. Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, wrote a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on Wednesday to express “serious concern” about reports involving a shortages of “basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns” onboard the Lincoln. According to reports from the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, citing family members and spouses of Sailors assigned to the Lincoln, people aboard the ship are suffering from exhaustion, suicidal thoughts and low morale, with some alleging that Sailors have made multiple attempts to jump overboard requiring intervention from other Servicemembers. Amid the wave of concerning reports from the Lincoln, Navy leadership met with the family of Sailors who are deployed aboard the Abraham Lincoln on Thursday in San Diego, listening to concerns and stories while pledging to support those onboard, according to Stars and Stripes.

headline: The U.S. is sending the USS George Washington (CVN-73) to the Middle East to replace USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72), according to U.S. officials cited by the Wall Street Journal. @WarshipCam published these images of the Washington, along with the Arleigh Burke class guided missile destroyer USS Shoup (DDG-86) and Ticonderoga class guided missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls (CG-62) transiting the Malacca Strait westbound earlier today. The Malacca Strait connects the Pacific and Indian oceans. The rotation comes as the Lincoln approaches 250+ days deployed and roughly 200 consecutive days without a port call. The carrier was originally scheduled to deploy in November 2025 but was redirected to the Middle East in January ahead of Operation Epic Fury. Since then, Lincoln and its air wing have supported the U.S. air campaign against Iran and the ongoing blockade of Iranian ports. The extended deployment is now drawing scrutiny from lawmakers over reported shortages of basic supplies, water and plumbing problems, mail disruptions, deck-safety concerns and deteriorating mental health among sailors. The Navy has not publicly confirmed the reported conditions. The carrier rotation itself, however, was reportedly planned before the concerns were raised. headline: The USS George Washington (CVN-73), USS Shoup (DDG-86) and USS Robert Smalls (CG-62) have transited the Singapore Strait westbound. The Washington is the flagship of Carrier Strike Group 5, the U.S. Navy's permanently forward deployed carrier strike group in the Indo-Pacific. A westbound transit through Singapore puts the group into the Indian Ocean, providing a potential route toward the Middle East without requiring movement through the Strait of Malacca's eastern approaches in the opposite direction. The movement comes as the USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) approaches its ninth month deployed with nearly a month's transit to get home and may provide some temporary relief until the USS Theodrore Roosevelt (CVN-71) deploys and arrives on station.
